Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Brit Pop Rivalry with Blur (1995)
facts.body: Oasis was deeply involved in an intense rivalry with Blur, described as a "war" between "Brit Pop's two biggest stars," which significantly hyped the release of Oasis's second album. The conflict began with a near-fight at a San Francisco radio station and escalated when Liam Gallagher and Damon Albarn almost brawled backstage at an award ceremony. Damon Albarn intentionally advanced Blur's single release date to coincide with Oasis's, culminating in the "Record War" of August 14, 1995, involving "Roll With It" versus "Country House," a battle that captivated all of Britain's music and daily papers, with even bookmakers taking bets. "This was much more than a rivalry. This was a war."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: The Chart War of August 1995
facts.body: Both Oasis and Blur planned album releases for Fall 1995: Blur's "The Great Escape" on September 11th and Oasis's "(What's the Story) Morning Glory" on October 2nd. The conflict escalated when Oasis announced their single "Roll With It" for August 14, 1995, and Blur subsequently announced their single "Country House" for release on the exact same day, setting up a direct competition for the number one spot. The media, bookies, and the public became heavily invested in this "Battle of Britpop." "Oasis announced that role with it would be released on August 14th, 1995. But then Blur announced that they too would release a single called Country House on that very same day."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Rockfield Studios Incident (May 1995)
facts.body: In May 1995, during the recording of their second album at Rockfield Studios in Wales, Liam returned from a pub extremely drunk with a large group of people from South Wales, who then invaded the studio causing damage. Noel locked the studio doors, embarrassing Liam, who subsequently battered Noel's bedroom door, breaking his foot. Noel retaliated by hitting Liam with a cricket bat, reportedly breaking Liam's arm, and then left the studio for a week to cool off. "Noel then grabbed a cricket bat, opened the door, and started whacking Liam with it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Rockfield Studios Fight – Cricket Bat Incident (May 1995)
facts.body: While recording their second album at Rockfield Studios in Wales, Liam brought a large, drunk group from a pub back to the studio, leading to damage. Noel locked the studio doors, embarrassing Liam. Later, Liam battered Noel's bedroom door, breaking his foot. Noel then grabbed a cricket bat, opened the door, and allegedly broke Liam's arm with it, subsequently leaving the studio for a week to calm down. "Noelle then grabbed a cricket bat, opened the door, and started walking Liam with it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Noel's Cricket Bat Auction (1995)
facts.body: The cricket bat that Noel Gallagher allegedly used to hit Liam Gallagher during the Rockfield Studios incident in May 1995 later came into the possession of music writer Paolo Huitt. Huitt subsequently auctioned the bat, complete with a certificate of authenticity, for approximately a thousand US dollars. "He later auctioned it off, complete with a certificate of authenticity. And I think it sold for about a thousand US dollars."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: "Battle of Britpop" Single Release - August 15, 1995
facts.body: Oasis's single "Roll With It" was deliberately released on August 15, 1995, the same day as Blur's "Country House," due to Damon Albarn's strategic move. This generated massive media attention, with even tabloids covering personal lives, the Financial Times running profiles, and the BBC covering it like a major news event. "Damon Alborn started it. When he found out when Oasis was going to release the first single from their What's the Story Morning Glory album, he moved the release date of the new Blur single up to the very same date, August 15th, 1995."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: "The Battle of Britpop" Competitor (August 1995)
facts.body: Oasis directly challenged Blur in August 1995 by moving the release of their single "Roll With It" to August 14, the same day as Blur's "Country House." Despite selling 216,000 copies, Oasis's single was outsold by Blur's. "Oasis said, no, we've decided that we're going to release our single in mid-August."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: "Overall War" Winner (1995)
facts.body: While Blur won the single battle, Oasis was the "clear winner" in the "overall war" of Britpop dominance in 1995, largely due to the monumental success of their album *What's the Story (Morning Glory)?* "But when it came to the overall war, Oasis was the clear winner."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: "Biggest Band on Planet Earth" (1995)
facts.body: For a period, Oasis achieved the status of "the biggest band on Planet Earth," a feat largely attributed to the immense global success of their album *What's the Story (Morning Glory)?* "Oasis, who for a time were the biggest band on Planet Earth. Thanks to their What's the Story Morning Glory album."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Tony McCarroll's Dismissal (April 30, 1995)
facts.body: Drummer Tony McCarroll was fired around April 30, 1995, receiving a call from the record label while visiting his mother. His dismissal stemmed from long-standing conflicts with Noel, Liam's dislike for him, and rumors of a physical fight. facts.title: Brit Pop Rivalry with Blur (1995)
facts.body: Oasis was deeply involved in an intense rivalry with Blur, described as a "war" between "Brit Pop's two biggest stars," which significantly hyped the release of Oasis's second album. The conflict began with a near-fight at a San Francisco radio station and escalated when Liam Gallagher and Damon Albarn almost brawled backstage at an award ceremony. Damon Albarn intentionally advanced Blur's single release date to coincide with Oasis's, culminating in the "Record War" of August 14, 1995, involving "Roll With It" versus "Country House," a battle that captivated all of Britain's music and daily papers, with even bookmakers taking bets. "This was much more than a rivalry. This was a war."

facts.title: Alan Wilder's Departure (June 1, 1995)
facts.body: On June 1, 1995, Alan Wilder officially left Depeche Mode, unable to tolerate the band's excesses, his limited role in songwriting, and his bandmates. The earlier fighter plane crash incident also contributed to his reassessment of his life and priorities. "On June 1st, 1995, Alan Wilder made it official. He could not take it anymore. He could not stand the excess. He could not stand not being able to write more of the music. And he could not stand any of his bandmates."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Dave Gahan's Near-Death Experience and Recovery (1995-1996)
facts.body: From late spring 1995 through to a brief clinical death in 1996, Dave Gahan's life was consumed by heroin addiction, costing $3,000 daily, leading to extreme dissociation, conversations with stuffed animals (including a Bugs Bunny doll), and two suicide attempts. On May 27, 1996, after an attempt to record with Martin Gore, Gahan injected cocaine and heroin at the Sunset Marquis Hotel in Hollywood, leading to full cardiac arrest and two minutes of clinical death. He recalled a vision of his wife screaming for him to return and a voice stating, "This is wrong, you don't get to decide." His recovery began after summer 1996, largely influenced by the threat of green card revocation from the American government if he didn't enter rehab and remain sober. He has been sober since June 6, 1996, now runs four times a week, lives in New York's West Village, and is married to Jennifer, his third wife. "He was for all intents and purposes clinically dead for two full minutes. He now says he remembers the vision of his wife screaming at him to come back to this plane."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: House Looting Post-Rehab (1995)
facts.body: After a period at a rehabilitation clinic in the Arizona desert, Dave Gahan was released on August 27, 1995. Upon returning to his house, he discovered it had been completely looted and burglarized. This incident immediately prompted him to use heroin ("smack") and check into the Sunset Marquis hotel. "But when he checked out on August 27, 1995 and returned to his house, he found that it had been completely looted, burgl'd."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Suicide Attempts and Overdose (1995-1996)
facts.body: While staying at the Sunset Marquis hotel in August 1995, Dave Gahan attempted suicide by slashing his wrists in the bathroom mirror. After waking in a psychiatric ward, his primary focus was getting high again, seemingly indifferent to the fact that a suicide attempt was a felony in California. He later made another unsuccessful attempt to hang himself in his bathroom. His struggles culminated on May 27, 1996, when after attending a party and checking back into the Sunset Marquis, he injected a mixture of heroin and cocaine, resulting in a massive overdose. At 1:15 AM on May 28, an unknown person called 911, and paramedics found him clinically dead for two minutes due to full cardiac arrest. "When he woke up in the psychiatric ward, all he could think about was getting high again."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Band's Low Point (1995)
facts.body: The year 1995 marked the lowest point for Depeche Mode, characterized by internal turmoil and severe personal crises among its members. Dave Gahan was battling a life-threatening heroin addiction, Martin Gore was struggling with alcoholism and personal relationship problems, and Alan Wilder, citing the "unsustainable situation," decided to leave the band. This period led to widespread speculation in the press that the band was finished or dissolved. "1995 fue posiblemente el momento más bajo de la banda y yo creo que fue ese momento en el que tocaron fondo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: US Justice Department Antitrust Inquiry (1995)
facts.body: In the period after their tour cancellation, the US Justice Department contacted Pearl Jam, having monitored Ticketmaster since its 1991 merger with Ticketron and being aware of Pearl Jam's disputes over service charges. The Justice Department reportedly encouraged Pearl Jam to file an antitrust complaint, rather than a lawsuit, initiating an investigation into Ticketmaster's practices. "It appears that the Justice Department may have encouraged Pearl Jam to file a complaint, not a lawsuit, asking for an antitrust investigation into ticket master's practices."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Antitrust Hearing and Inconclusive Outcome (June 1995)
facts.body: A hearing was scheduled for Thursday, June 30, 1995, in Washington D.C., where members of Pearl Jam's organization and supportive music industry figures presented their case against Ticketmaster. Despite intense media coverage, the government's investigation was closed later in 1995 without any substantial action, with only a promise for continued monitoring of the ticketing industry. "But in the end, nothing came of it. The government investigation was closed in 1995 without anyone doing anything."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Peak and Overexposure (Mid-1995)
facts.body: The Britpop party started to peak in the summer of 1995, fueled by rivalries like the Blur vs. Oasis chart war. However, it also suffered from overexposure, with every indie label "throwing bands against the wall," and major players like Oasis constantly in the press, even detailing Noel Gallagher's wife's shopping sprees. "The party started to peak in the summer of 1995, and the best part was the war between blur and oasis."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Decline Factors (Late 1995-1997)
facts.body: The genre began to get "wobbly" due to a loss of focus with too many mediocre bands, criminal overexposure of its stars, the pressure for follow-up albums to *Parklife* and *Morning Glory*, and rampant drug use (heroin and cocaine) taking its toll on musicians and the industry. "First of all, everybody was starting to lose focus."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Peak and Inevitable Decline - Summer 1995
facts.body: Britpop reached its peak in the summer of 1995, followed by an "inevitable decline." The momentum initially masked the cracks, but signs like BBC Radio 1's policy shift and the University of Leeds symposium on Britpop reflected its widespread influence before the downturn. "The peak of Britpop was the summer of 1995. After that came the long, slow, inevitable decline."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Peak and Media Frenzy (Summer 1995)
facts.body: Britpop reached its peak in the summer of 1995, characterized by non-stop media coverage across print, radio, and TV, widespread paparazzi and gossip, and even a *Vanity Fair* feature on "Cool Britannia and Swing in London." "The party reached its peak in the summer of 1995."

facts.title: Post-Peak Decline (Late 1995)
facts.body: After reaching its peak in 1995, particularly with the massive success of Oasis's *What's the Story (Morning Glory)?*, Britpop could "not possibly get any bigger," signaling that its trajectory was inevitably "down." "Britpop itself could not possibly get any bigger. So you know what that means, right? There was only one direction left to go. Down."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Wobbling and Decline (1995-1996)
facts.body: As 1995 transitioned into 1996, Britpop began to show signs of instability and "getting a little wobbly," indicating the natural progression of a cultural storm reaching its end. "And as 1995 turned into 1996, it became apparent that Britpop was getting a little wobbly."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Golden Age (1995)
facts.body: The Britpop movement reached its full peak and golden age around 1995, marked by significant album releases like Blur's "Parklife" (April 1994) and Oasis's "(What's the Story) Morning Glory?" (August 1995), which propelled the movement to its highest point of popularity and influence.
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: The Great Battle of Britpop (1995)
facts.body: The "Great Battle of Britpop," particularly highlighted by the simultaneous single releases of Oasis and Blur in 1995, was critically dismissed as a "discographic nonsense" or marketing ploy. Despite this, it became a significant cultural event, with Oasis ultimately "winning" in terms of sales and public recognition. "todo eso de la gran batería de ripop pero una patraña discográfica."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Decline Factors (Late 1995-1997)
facts.body: The genre began to get "wobbly" due to a loss of focus with too many mediocre bands, criminal overexposure of its stars, the pressure for follow-up albums to *Parklife* and *Morning Glory*, and rampant drug use (heroin and cocaine) taking its toll on musicians and the industry. "First of all, everybody was starting to lose focus."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Peak and Inevitable Decline - Summer 1995
facts.body: Britpop reached its peak in the summer of 1995, followed by an "inevitable decline." The momentum initially masked the cracks, but signs like BBC Radio 1's policy shift and the University of Leeds symposium on Britpop reflected its widespread influence before the downturn. "The peak of Britpop was the summer of 1995. After that came the long, slow, inevitable decline."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Peak and Media Frenzy (Summer 1995)
facts.body: Britpop reached its peak in the summer of 1995, characterized by non-stop media coverage across print, radio, and TV, widespread paparazzi and gossip, and even a *Vanity Fair* feature on "Cool Britannia and Swing in London." "The party reached its peak in the summer of 1995."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Peak and Overexposure (Mid-1995)
facts.body: The Britpop party started to peak in the summer of 1995, fueled by rivalries like the Blur vs. Oasis chart war. However, it also suffered from overexposure, with every indie label "throwing bands against the wall," and major players like Oasis constantly in the press, even detailing Noel Gallagher's wife's shopping sprees. "The party started to peak in the summer of 1995, and the best part was the war between blur and oasis."

facts.title: Drug Treatment Agreement (May 1995)
facts.body: Following his May 1995 drug bust, Wyland was informed by the court that he could avoid a criminal record if he successfully completed a drug treatment program, a condition he agreed to. "Wyland was told that if he completed a drug treatment program, he would be free to go without a criminal record."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Pasadena Drug Bust (May 15, 1995)
facts.body: At approximately 3:30 AM on Monday, May 15, 1995, in Pasadena, California, Scott Wyland was apprehended by police after being seen leaving the rear of a CD motel with his lights off. Officers, suspecting a drug transaction, found a chunk of Mexican black tar heroin in his wallet upon apprehension. "When they caught up with Scott, the cops found a chunk of Mexican black tar heroin in Wyland's wallet."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Post-Arrest Drug Seeking (May 15, 1995)
facts.body: Immediately after being released on $10,000 bail (posted by his wife), Scott Wyland demanded that Janina drive him to his dealer's house to "score" drugs. When she refused, he jumped out of their 1965 Mustang while it was moving at 15-20 miles per hour. "When she refused, Scott jumped out of the car while it was still moving at 15 or 20 miles an hour."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Public Statement of Remorse (May 1995)
facts.body: While at the Chateau Marmont, Scott Wyland prepared a tearful statement of remorse which Courtney Love then called a local radio station in the middle of the night to read live on air. In the statement, he apologized to his friends, band, wife, family, and acknowledged becoming a "hypocrite" to social ideals, expressing a desire to recover and create more music. "I have a disease it went. I want to say sorry to my friends, my band, my wife, and my family and to the social ideals to which I have become a hypocrite. I ache to get well, to feel, and to make more music."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Rehab in Colorado (Summer 1995)
facts.body: Scott Wyland spent part of the summer of 1995 at a rehabilitation facility located in Colorado, returning to Los Angeles by the end of August that year. "He agreed and spent part of that summer at a rehab facility in Colorado."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Seeking Solace with Courtney Love (May 1995)
facts.body: After Janina refused to allow him back home following his arrest and subsequent behavior, Scott Wyland sought refuge with Courtney Love, who was staying at the Chateau Marmont Hotel on Sunset Boulevard. "When Jeanine refused to let Scott come home, he sought solace in of all people, Courtney Love, who had a room with the Chateau Marmont Hotel on sunset bullifard."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Dual Brain Aneurysms – March 1, 1995, Lausanne, Switzerland, Emergency Surgery; Tour Resumed May 15
facts.body: Ninety minutes into the 27th show of the Monster world tour — which had started on November 13, 1994 in Perth, Australia — drummer Bill Berry felt as if "somebody dropped a bowling ball on his head" and had to be carried from the stage in Lausanne, Switzerland. He had suffered not one but two potentially fatal brain aneurysms. Emergency brain surgery was performed, and Berry spent eight weeks recovering with the outcome uncertain. The tour was postponed; it resumed on May 15 in San Francisco. To demonstrate the band's dark humor about the episode, the tour program subsequently featured an X-ray of Bill's head showing where the aneurysms had been. "It was not one, but two potentially fatal brain aneurysms."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Bill Berry's Brain Aneurysms (March 1995)
facts.body: On March 1, 1995, during a Monster Tour stop in Lausanne, Switzerland, ninety minutes into the set, Bill Berry was suddenly afflicted by a headache so intense he described it as if "somebody had dropped the bowling ball on a skull," and he had to be carried off stage. Initially thought to be a severe migraine caused by stress and the high altitude of the Swiss Alps, a subsequent CAT scan revealed two potentially fatal brain aneurysms. Bill underwent emergency brain surgery and endured an eight-week recovery period, during which there were serious concerns about potential brain damage affecting his ability to speak or remember. "Bill was rushed in for emergency brain surgery and he spent eight long weeks recovering."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: 1995 World Tour Incident
facts.body: In January 1995, R.E.M. embarked on their first world tour in six years, beginning in Australia and moving through Asia before reaching Europe. During a show on March 1, 1995, at the Demali Ice Rink in Lausanne, Switzerland, drummer Bill Berry collapsed on stage about 90 minutes into the gig while singing a falsetto part in the song "Tongue." "During that show, Bill developed a bad headache... And then about 90 minutes into the gig as he was singing the falsetto part in a song called Tung, Bill recalls feeling like somebody dropped the bowling ball on his head."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Sells Half of ATV Music to Sony (1995)
facts.body: Facing financial difficulties, Jackson sold half of his ATV Music catalog to Sony Music in 1995 for approximately $100 million, representing a substantial return on his initial investment. "Jackson was having financial issues, so he sold half of this catalog to Sony Music for about $100 million. So very nice return on investment."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Michael Jackson

facts.title: Rehab and Jail Stints (1995-1998)
facts.body: Throughout 1995, Scott Weiland was frequently in and out of rehab and jail. In 1998, he was arrested on a possession charge and sentenced to a year in jail. "During 1995 Wyland was in and out of rehab and in and out of jail. And then in 1998 he was nabbed on a possession charge and sentenced to a year in jail."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Stone Temple Pilots

facts.title: Weiland's Legal Issues (1995-2008)
facts.body: Weiland's legal troubles began in 1995 with an arrest for attempting to buy crack. In 1998, he was jailed for a possession charge. In December 2007, he received another DUI charge, resulting in an 18-month alcohol rehab program, four years probation, and eight days in jail (of which he served about 10 hours). He attended rehab for three weeks in January 2008. "Starting in 1995, Wyland was in and out of rehab and in and out of jail, starting with a bust involving an attempt to buy some crack."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Stone Temple Pilots

facts.title: Brit Pop Rivalry with Oasis (1995)
facts.body: Blur's rivalry with Oasis escalated into a "Record War" in August 1995, representing the peak of Brit Pop. This intense competition involved "Brit Pop's two biggest stars going at each other's throats," starting with a near-fight at a San Francisco radio station and an almost-brawl between Damon Albarn and Liam Gallagher backstage at an award ceremony. Damon Albarn deliberately moved up Blur's new single release date to clash with Oasis's, setting the stage for a nationwide sensation where all music papers, magazines, and daily papers covered the battle, and bookmakers even took bets on which single would achieve the number one spot. "The Blur versus Oasis Record War, with the height of Brit Pop in August of 1995."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: The Chart War of August 1995
facts.body: Blur strategically scheduled the release of their single "Country House" for August 14, 1995, the same day Oasis was releasing "Roll With It." This intentional clash sparked the "Battle of Britpop," captivating the entire UK, with bookmakers even laying odds on the outcome. "But then Blur announced that they too would release a single called Country House on that very same day."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: Initiation of "Battle of Britpop" - August 15, 1995
facts.body: Damon Albarn deliberately escalated the rivalry with Oasis by moving the release date of a new Blur single ("Country House") to August 15, 1995, the exact same day Oasis was releasing their single ("Roll With It"). This move triggered a massive media frenzy and the iconic "Battle of Britpop." "Damon Alborn started it. When he found out when Oasis was going to release the first single from their What's the Story Morning Glory album, he moved the release date of the new Blur single up to the very same date, August 15th, 1995."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: "The Battle of Britpop" Winner (August 1995)
facts.body: Blur emerged victorious in the direct chart showdown against Oasis in August 1995. By moving "Country House" to release on the same day as Oasis's "Roll With It" (August 14, 1995), Blur sold 274,000 copies, surpassing Oasis's 216,000 and claiming the number one spot. "Blur, the winners of the epic Britpop showdown of August 1995."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: Fatigue and Disillusionment (1995)
facts.body: By 1995, as Britpop reached its peak, Blur, despite their success, arrived with a different attitude compared to fresh, younger bands like Oasis. They were fatigued from extensive touring, tired of record label pressure (specifically from EMI), disillusioned with the music industry, and experiencing internal problems, feeling like "old dogs" in the movement.
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: Early Career Weariness (1995)
facts.body: By 1995, Blur was described as being "burnt out" after four or five years in the market, having released several albums, faced various economic issues, and grown quite disillusioned with the recording industry. "Blur llegaba a 1995, ya relativamente quemado, 4 o 5 años en el mercado había sacado varios iscos, había estado ya con varios temas económicos, había estado bastante desencantado con aiscografica."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: Veteran Status in Britpop Battle (1995)
facts.body: By the time of the "Great Britpop Battle" in 1995, Blur possessed a veteran status, having already navigated early career struggles, stylistic shifts, and financial difficulties. This experience made them less eager to fully participate in the media-fueled rivalry compared to the younger, more pressured Oasis. "Blur que habían empezado antes y ya habían tenido sus problemas, sus tumbos se habían arruinado, ya eran un poco perro viejo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Blur

facts.title: Early Legal Download Example (1995)
facts.body: Sonic Youth's music was offered as an example of the first legal downloadable music provided by Sonic Net in mid-1995. These early downloads were characterized by variable audio quality, sometimes described as only "a little better than a bad AM radio," due to the nascent stage of digital music distribution before widespread MP3 adoption. "Sonic Youth, an example of what some of the first legal downloadable music sounded like, when Sonic Net became the first company to offer such a thing in the middle of 1995."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10
facts.name: Sonic Youth

facts.title: First Demo Tape (May 1995) – Cassette Worth ~$1,000 Today
facts.body: In May 1995, the band recorded four songs possibly under the guidance of Matt's father George ("Copyright Geo Bell Music" appears on the cassette label). The tape, titled *This Is a Muse Demo*, was distributed to promoters and venues across the northwest of England by their first manager Phil Corthals, securing more gigs and their first overseas show (in France). Very few copies were made; the cassette now sells for close to $1,000. "If you can find one, the asking price is close to $1,000."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Muse

facts.title: Wipeout Soundtrack Contribution (1995)
facts.body: The Chemical Brothers were among the reputable artists from the British club scene whose licensed music was featured in the futuristic racing game Wipeout. This collaboration was part of an atypical promotional strategy, where playable game units were installed in UK clubs before the PlayStation's market release, marking a significant shift in video game soundtracks towards licensed electronic music. "Por primera vez, un juego contaba con la música licenciada de artistas reputados de la escena de club británica."
facts.source: Central Sonora

facts.title: Post-Twice Removed Breakup Rumors (1995)
facts.body: In late 1994 and early 1995, rumors of Sloan disbanding spread, culminating in an April 1st, 1995 newswire story. Reasons cited by manager Chip Sutherland included Geffen's perceived inadequate US promotion, Andrew Scott's move to Toronto, and the band's reluctance to continue under a major label contract. Chris Murphy even announced a Halifax show as their last. "After twice removed, things began to, well, they began to fall apart. This was when the breakup rumors started. On April 1st, 1995, a story was carried on the newswire. Sloan disbands Halifax, Grunge Pop's sensation may be calling it quits."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1
facts.name: Sloan

facts.title: Rockfield Studio Embarrassment (May 1995)
facts.body: During recording sessions at Rockfield Studios, Liam returned from the pub drunk with a large group of people who invaded the studio. Noel locked the doors, preventing Liam's entourage from entering, which deeply embarrassed Liam as he felt "told off" by his older brother in front of his friends. "Noel locked the studio doors and no one could get in, which really embarrassed Liam."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Liam Gallagher

facts.title: Foot Injury (May 1995)
facts.body: Following his embarrassment at Rockfield Studios, Liam, in a fit of rage, began battering Noel's bedroom door, breaking his own foot in the process. "So when everybody finally left, Liam began battering Noel's bedroom door, breaking his foot in the process."

facts.title: Scene Reputation and Evolution to Drama Bass (1995)
facts.body: Despite its growing popularity, jungle's reputation suffered by 1995 as the scene became associated with increased physicality, harder drugs, fights, and conflicts. This negative perception led several musicians to distance themselves and refine the jungle sound, which eventually gave birth to drum and bass. "A la aumentar la velocidad de la intensidad, la escena se volvió mucho más física, entraron drogas más duras y fue común ver peleas y conflictos."

facts.title: Pre-Disappearance Behavior (January 1995)
facts.body: After his dog's death, Richie shaved off all his hair and began acting even more strangely than usual, despite being off alcohol and drugs. On January 31, he and bandmate James Dean Bradfield checked into the London Embassy Hotel in preparation for a North American promotional trip. "After that, Richie shaved off all his hair and began acting even more strangely than usual, even though he was off alcohol and drugs at that point. On January 31, he and bandmate James Dean Bradford checked into the London Embassy Hotel on Bayes Water Road, which is right across the street from High Park in London. The purpose was to get ready for a promotional trip through North America."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Manic Street Preachers

facts.title: Last Known Contact (January 31, 1995)
facts.body: At 8:30 PM on January 31, James Dean Bradfield knocked on Richie's door, room 561, but Richie politely declined to go out, stating he was about to take a bath. He later called his mother, expressing reservations about the upcoming trip to America but acknowledging it as a necessary part of being in a rock band; this was the last time anyone heard from him. "At 8.30 that night, James knocked on Richie's door, room 561, and asked if he wanted to go out. Richie politely declined, saying that he was just about to have a bath. He later called his mother to say that he wasn't wild about having to go to America, but at the same time, he understood it was something people and rock bands have to do from time to time. And that was the last anyone heard from him."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Manic Street Preachers

facts.title: Disappearance Details (February 1, 1995)
facts.body: At 7 AM on February 1, 1995, Richie checked out of the hotel and drove his Vauxhall Cavalier to his home in Cardiff, Wales, where he left belongings, including his Prozac bottle and passport, on his desk. Over the previous two weeks, he had withdrawn £200 daily, totaling £2800, for unknown purposes, possibly for the US tour or a new desk he had seen in Cardiff. "At 7am on February 1, 1995, Richie checked out of the hotel and drove his voxol cabalier to his home in Cardiff Wales, where he dropped off some stuff, including his bottle of Prozac. And he also left his passport, which he left right on the desk. As for money, well, for the past two weeks, Richie had been withdrawing 200 pounds a day from his bank account, taking out a total of 2800 pounds. What was he using that money for? No idea. It could have been for the US tour, although he talked about buying a new desk for his home. He'd found it in a shop in Cardiff, but he never bought it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Manic Street Preachers

facts.title: Alleged Sightings and Car Discovery (February 1995)
facts.body: On February 7, a cab driver allegedly picked Richie up from a hotel in Newport and drove him for £68 cash. About a week later, a fan reportedly spoke to him at a Newport bus station, and he was allegedly seen at a passport office. On February 14, Richie's car was found at the Aust Service Station by the Severn Bridge, a known suicide spot, with a parking ticket and reported as abandoned three days later. "On February 7, a cab driver allegedly picked him up from a hotel in the well-city of Newport and drove him around for a bit. The ride cost 68 pounds, which the passenger paid in cash. Then, a fan apparently talked to him about a week later at a bus station in the well-city of Newport. He was also allegedly seen at a passport office. Richie's car was found on February 14 that the nearby Austin Service Station by the Severin Bridge, which is supposedly a favorite spot for those seeking suicide. It had gotten a ticket for illegal parking. Three days later, it was reported as abandoned."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Manic Street Preachers

facts.title: Richie Edwards' Disappearance (1995)
facts.body: Richie Edwards, an extreme member of the Manic Street Preachers known for depression, anorexia, drug use, and self-mutilation, disappeared on February 1, 1995, following the death of his dog on January 14, 1995. On January 31, 1995, he checked into a London hotel with James Dean Bradfield, declined to go out, and later called his mom expressing reluctance about an upcoming North American promo tour; he checked out at 7 AM on February 1st, drove to his Cardiff, Wales home to drop off Prozac and his passport, and his car was found 12 days later by a country bridge with a dead battery. No body, clues, or motives were ever found, leading to his legal declaration of death on February 1, 2002, though "Elvis-like sightings" continued in various locations. "What happened to Richie Edwards on February 1st, 1995?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2
facts.name: Manic Street Preachers

facts.title: Disappearance from Embassy Hotel (January 31 - February 1, 1995)
facts.body: After a final rehearsal with the band on January 31, 1995, Richie gave small presents to his bandmates, possibly as an apology. He then checked into the Embassy Hotel in London with James Dean Bradfield. Richie was last seen by James Dean Bradfield at approximately 8:30 pm on January 31, 1995, in his room (516), taking a bath and stating he would spend a quiet night alone, before he vanished completely by February 1, 1995. "James Dean Bradfield may have been the last person to see Richie alive. This brings us to February 1, 1995. What happened? Well, we'll explore that next."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

facts.title: Rise of Pop Music (Late 1995)
facts.body: By the end of 1995, pop music, including the Spice Girls, began to grab attention in North America, pushing alternative rock to the margins. "pop music, you know, the Spice Girls and Inksink and the Backstreet Boys all started to grab the attention in North America."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Spice Girls

facts.title: Rise of Pop Music (Late 1995)
facts.body: The Spice Girls were among the pop artists that defined the musical tastes of Generation Y towards the end of the 1990s, reflecting a shift away from brooding grunge and post-punk alt-rock. "This cheerful generation led us to an era of spice girls and backstreet boys in sync, Britney Spears."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Emergence (Late 1995)
facts.body: Nu Metal emerged after 1995 as Alt Rock fragmented, characterized as an "overly aggressive and not too bright fusion of heavy metal and hip hop." "This is where we encounter new metal, which in retrospect was an overly aggressive and not too bright fusion of heavy metal and hip hop."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nu Metal

facts.title: Drummer for Alanis Morissette (1995)
facts.body: After Alanis Morissette's "Jagged Little Pill" album blew up in 1995, Taylor Hawkins became her drummer at age 23 for her "Can't Not" tour. He appeared in several of her music videos and performed with her during her debut on David Letterman in 1995. "That Sass Jordan job morphed into a gig with Alannis Morissette."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Taylor Hawkins

facts.title: Lo-Fi Offshoot Subgenre (Post-1995)
facts.body: Identified as an offshoot subgenre of low-fidelity music that emerged after 1995, Chillwave represents the broadening impact and stylistic diversification of the lo-fi aesthetic. Its development illustrates how the foundational principles of lo-fi continued to inspire new musical movements and sounds. "Low five became such an established mindset and process that it began to spawn offshoot subgenres, such as hip-negogic pop and chill wave and glow five."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: First Hiatus (1995-1996)
facts.body: From September 1995 to some time in 1996, the band experienced a period that appeared to be a dissolution but was later considered a hiatus rather than a formal breakup. "There was a time from September 1995 to some time in 1996 where it looked like they were done, but they weren't."

facts.title: Encounter with Fred Durst (Early 1995)
facts.body: In early 1995, while Korn was on tour promoting their recently released debut album, they encountered Fred Durst in Jacksonville, Florida. Durst, a tattoo artist and an ardent fan, offered the band members free tattoos. "In early 1995, Corn was on a tour that brought them through town."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

facts.title: Existential Moment: Dropped by Warner (c. 1995)
facts.body: After the release of their sixth album, "Smiling Buddha Cabaret," the band was dropped by their American label, Warner. This presented an "existential moment" where they considered quitting but ultimately decided to continue on their own terms rather than following external pressures. "Another existential moment. Another moment where you could pack it in or decide you're going to go on."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Transition Period and Songwriting Volume (c. 1995-1997)
facts.body: During the period after being dropped by Warner and before signing with Sony Music Canada, the band entered a "couple of years" of transition, actively writing a large volume of songs. For a potential record (referred to as "dear, dear record"), they had accumulated approximately 30 to 40 songs. "Drew, we must have had 30 or 40 songs. We have about 30 songs for the dear, dear record."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Relationship with Paula Yates and Tabloid Coverage (1995-1997)
facts.body: Hutchence was involved in a complex and unhealthy breakup with British TV personality Paula Yates, the mother of his children, by 1995. Their relationship was characterized by extensive drug and alcohol use and became a prominent subject of tabloid coverage. "By 1995, he was locked into a complex breakup with Paula Yates, the British TV person."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Michael Hutchence

facts.title: Split from Helena Christensen (March 1995)
facts.body: He separated from Helena Christensen in March 1995 after being discovered with Paula Yates in a hotel, a development that became a major tabloid sensation in England. "Hutchinson, Christianson, split up after he was caught with Yates in a hotel."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
